name: French criminal procedure knowledge base (English paraphrases) for the LCCC agents
disclaimer: Plain-English paraphrases written for a hackathon prototype. They are not official translations. Every entry must be checked against Legifrance before any real use. Entries marked 'web-checked' were cross-checked online on 2026-10-04; the others come from domain knowledge.

entries.title: Flagrant offence investigation (enquete de flagrance): duration
entries.text: A flagrance investigation can be carried out without interruption for 8 days from the offence. If the investigation cannot be deferred and the offence is punishable by at least 5 years' imprisonment, the Public Prosecutor may extend it once for a further 8 days (16 days in total).

extension.condition: offence punishable by 5+ years and investigation cannot be deferred

deadline.actor: Judicial police under the direction of the Public Prosecutor

entries.risk: Acts performed under flagrance rules after the deadline (without extension) may be annulled.

entries.title: Scene examination by the judicial police officer
entries.text: In a flagrant felony, the judicial police officer informs the Public Prosecutor immediately, goes to the scene without delay, makes all useful findings and preserves the evidence likely to disappear.
entries.risk: Missing or late scene report weakens the chain of evidence.

entries.title: Searches and seizures: inventory and sealing of exhibits
entries.text: Objects and documents seized are immediately inventoried and placed under seal (scelle). The chain of custody of seals must be traceable from seizure to analysis; any discrepancy in seal numbering or description must be explained.
entries.risk: A broken or inconsistent chain of custody may lead to the annulment of the seizure and of the expert analysis based on it.

entries.title: Search of a home: presence of the occupant or two witnesses
entries.text: A search of a home takes place in the presence of the person concerned or, failing that, of a representative or two witnesses chosen by the officer. The report and the inventory are signed by them.
entries.risk: A search without the required persons present is a classic ground for nullity.

entries.title: Search hours
entries.text: Except in specific cases (request from inside the premises, organised crime regimes, emergencies provided by law), home searches cannot begin before 6 a.m. or after 9 p.m.
entries.risk: A night-time search outside the legal exceptions may be annulled.

entries.title: Requisitions for information (telephone records, CCTV, documents)
entries.text: The officer may require any person, body or operator to hand over information useful to the investigation, including telephone billing records and video recordings.

entries.title: Police custody (garde a vue): conditions
entries.text: Custody is a measure of constraint decided by a judicial police officer under the control of the judicial authority, against a person suspected on plausible grounds of an offence punishable by imprisonment, when it is the only way to achieve one of the objectives listed by law.

entries.title: Police custody: duration, extension and start time
entries.text: Custody cannot exceed 24 hours. It can be extended once for 24 more hours (48 hours in total) by written and reasoned authorisation of the Public Prosecutor, for offences punishable by at least one year's imprisonment. The start time of the measure is, where applicable, the time at which the person was apprehended (Art. 63, III).

extension.condition: written and reasoned authorisation before the first 24 hours expire

deadline.actor: Judicial police officer under prosecutor control

entries.risk: A start time later than the apprehension, or an extension authorised after expiry, may ground a nullity request against the custody and the statements taken.

entries.title: Custody: immediate notification of rights
entries.text: The person placed in custody is immediately informed of the placement, its duration and extensions, the offence, and of the rights to inform a relative and employer, to a medical examination, to a lawyer, to an interpreter, to consult certain documents and to remain silent.
entries.risk: Late notification of rights is a frequent ground for nullity.

entries.title: Custody: assistance of a lawyer
entries.text: From the start of custody the person may ask to be assisted by a lawyer. Hearings cannot start, except in urgent cases authorised by law, before a 2-hour period following the notice to the lawyer.

entries.title: Extended custody (up to 96 hours) for organised crime only
entries.text: Custody can exceptionally be extended by two further periods of 24 hours (96 hours in total) only for offences listed in Art. 706-73 (for example murder committed by an organised gang). An ordinary murder, without organised-gang elements, stays within the 48-hour ceiling of Art. 63.

deadline.actor: Judge (JLD or investigating judge) authorises the additional periods

entries.risk: Applying the 96-hour regime to an offence outside Art. 706-73 makes the custody beyond 48 hours irregular.

entries.title: Discovery of a body
entries.text: When a body is discovered and the cause of death is unknown or suspicious, the officer informs the Public Prosecutor, who may go to the scene and order forensic examinations. When the death is clearly violent, the flagrance regime applies.

entries.title: Judicial autopsy and return of the body
entries.text: A judicial autopsy is ordered by the Public Prosecutor or the investigating judge and carried out by a forensic doctor. Since the law of 23 July 2026 (JCRV), relatives are informed that an autopsy was ordered, and the body is in principle returned to the family within one month of the autopsy, unless public-health constraints or the needs of the investigation require otherwise.

entries.title: Judicial investigation is mandatory for felonies; opening by the prosecutor
entries.text: A judicial investigation (information judiciaire) is mandatory for felonies such as murder. It is opened by the Public Prosecutor's introductory submission (requisitoire introductif) to the investigating judge.

entries.title: Placement under formal investigation (mise en examen)
entries.text: The investigating judge can place under formal investigation only persons against whom there is serious or corroborating evidence making it likely that they took part in the offence.

entries.title: Investigation for and against; mandatory personality inquiry for felonies
entries.text: The investigating judge carries out every act useful to establish the truth, looking for evidence both against and in favour of the person. In felony cases, a personality inquiry on the person under formal investigation (material, family and social situation) is mandatory.

entries.title: Requests for investigative acts by the parties
entries.text: Parties may ask in writing for a hearing, an interrogation or any useful act. If the judge does not grant the request, a reasoned order must be issued within one month of receipt. In addition, when four months have passed since the last appearance of the person under formal investigation, that person may request an interrogation, which the judge must carry out within 30 days of receipt of the request.

deadline.trigger: receipt of the written request at the court registry

extra.trigger: receipt of an interrogation request after 4 months without appearance

entries.risk: No answer within the time limit allows the party to refer the matter to the president of the investigation chamber.

entries.title: First appearance before the investigating judge
entries.text: At the first appearance, the judge informs the person of the facts, of the right to remain silent, to make statements or to answer questions, and of the right to a lawyer, before deciding on formal investigation.

entries.title: Pre-trial detention: exceptional and reasoned
entries.text: Liberty is the rule. Pre-trial detention can only be ordered if it is the only way to achieve one of the objectives listed in Art. 144 (preserving evidence, preventing pressure on witnesses or collusion, protecting the person, ensuring appearance, ending the disturbance to public order in felony cases) and if judicial supervision or electronic house arrest would be insufficient.

entries.title: Pre-trial detention in felony cases: duration and ceilings
entries.text: In felony cases, detention cannot initially exceed one year. The liberty and detention judge (JLD) may extend it by periods of up to six months after an adversarial hearing. The total cannot exceed two years when the sentence incurred is below 20 years, and three years otherwise (four years in certain cases, such as offences committed abroad or organised crime).

extension.condition: reasoned order after adversarial hearing, before expiry

deadline.actor: JLD, on referral by the investigating judge; the prosecutor files submissions

entries.risk: Detention continued without a valid extension order before expiry is unlawful and leads to release.

entries.title: Request for release (demande de mise en liberte)
entries.text: The request is sent to the investigating judge, who immediately forwards the file to the Public Prosecutor for submissions. Unless the judge grants it, the judge must forward it with a reasoned opinion to the JLD within 5 days of the communication to the prosecutor. The JLD rules within 3 working days; failing that, the person may refer the request directly to the investigation chamber. The law of 23 July 2026 adds that a new request cannot be filed while a previous one is pending.

deadline.trigger: communication of the request to the Public Prosecutor
deadline.actor: Investigating judge (then JLD within 3 working days)

entries.risk: Missing the deadline lets the person refer the case directly to the investigation chamber and may lead to release.

entries.title: Expert opinions: appointment and time limit
entries.text: When a technical question arises, the investigating judge may order an expert opinion. The order appointing the expert sets a time limit for filing the report, which may be extended on reasoned request.

entries.title: Notification of expert conclusions to the parties
entries.text: The judge notifies the expert conclusions to the parties and their lawyers and sets a time limit within which they may submit observations or ask for further or counter expert opinions.

entries.title: Procedural nullity: substantial formality and harm
entries.text: There is nullity when a substantial formality provided by law has been disregarded and this has harmed the interests of the party concerned (no nullity without harm, Art. 802).

entries.title: Time limit for nullity requests during the judicial investigation
entries.text: The person under formal investigation must raise nullities of acts performed before the first appearance within six months of being placed under formal investigation (the same applies after each later interrogation for the acts preceding it). The law of 23 July 2026 reduces this time limit to four months; its date of entry into force must be checked.
entries.risk: Custody or search irregularities can be raised by the defence during this window.

entries.title: Notice of end of investigation and final submissions
entries.text: When the investigation appears complete, the judge notifies the parties and sends the file to the prosecutor. Parties then have one month if a person under investigation is detained (three months otherwise) to submit observations, request acts or raise nullities; the prosecutor files final submissions within the same time limit.

deadline.trigger: notice of end of investigation (detained person)
deadline.alt: 3 months if no one is detained

entries.title: Computation of time limits
entries.text: Every time limit expires on its last day at midnight. A time limit that would expire on a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday is extended to the next working day.

entries.title: Appeal against an Assize Court verdict
entries.text: The accused, the Public Prosecutor and the civil party (on civil interests) may appeal a conviction by the Assize Court. The appeal must be lodged within 10 days of the pronouncement of the verdict; the case is then retried by another Assize Court.

entries.title: Appeal to the Court of Cassation (pourvoi)
entries.text: The Public Prosecutor and all parties have five clear days after the day the decision was pronounced to lodge an appeal on points of law with the Court of Cassation. (Art. 576 concerns the form of the declaration, not the time limit.)

deadline.trigger: day after the pronouncement of the decision

entries.title: Murder (meurtre)
entries.text: Intentionally causing the death of another person is murder, punishable by 30 years' criminal imprisonment. Intent to kill is usually inferred from the weapon, the number and location of blows (vital areas), and their violence.

entries.title: Premeditated murder (assassinat)
entries.text: Murder committed with premeditation or by ambush is punishable by life imprisonment. Premeditation is the plan formed before the act (Art. 132-72); typical indicators are a weapon brought to the scene, reconnaissance, preparations or an ambush.

entries.title: Murder linked to another offence
entries.text: Murder that precedes, accompanies or follows another felony, or that aims to prepare or facilitate a misdemeanour (such as theft) or the escape or impunity of its author, is punishable by life imprisonment. (This is Art. 221-2, not Art. 221-4.)

entries.title: Aggravating circumstances of murder
entries.text: Murder is punishable by life imprisonment when committed, among other cases, against a minor under 15, a particularly vulnerable person, a spouse or former spouse, a police officer or other person holding public authority, a witness or victim to prevent a complaint or testimony, or by an organised gang.

entries.title: Violence causing death without intent to kill
entries.text: Intentional violence that causes death without intent to kill is punishable by 15 years' criminal imprisonment, raised to 20 years with an aggravating circumstance, notably the use or threat of a weapon (such as a knife).

entries.title: Self-defence
entries.text: A person who, faced with an unjustified attack on themselves or another, performs at the same time an act required by the need for self-defence is not criminally liable, unless the means used are disproportionate to the seriousness of the attack. Indicators: injuries on the suspect, weapon held by the victim, entry of the victim into the suspect's home.

entries.title: Mental disorder: abolished or impaired discernment
entries.text: A person whose discernment was abolished by a psychiatric or neuropsychological disorder at the time of the act is not criminally liable. If discernment was only impaired, the person remains liable but the maximum sentence is reduced by one third (or, for life imprisonment, to 30 years). A psychiatric expert opinion is the usual source.

entries.title: Individualisation of the sentence
entries.text: Within the legal maximum, the sentence is set according to the circumstances of the offence and the personality of the offender, as well as their material, family and social situation.

entries.title: Legal recidivism for felonies
entries.text: A person already finally convicted of a felony, or of a misdemeanour punishable by 10 years' imprisonment, who commits a felony is a legal recidivist: the maximum sentence is raised (for example to life imprisonment when the felony is punishable by 20 or 30 years). The criminal record (bulletin no.1) is the source.

entries.title: Theft
entries.text: Theft is the fraudulent taking of another's property, punishable by 3 years' imprisonment and a fine (more when aggravated).

entries.title: Tampering with a crime scene or destroying evidence
entries.text: Altering the scene of a felony or misdemeanour, or destroying, concealing or cleaning traces or evidence, in order to obstruct the discovery of the truth, is a separate offence (3 years' imprisonment).
